title: 1 Samuel 2:11–17
context: Samuel begins serving the LORD before Eli, while Eli’s sons, who do not know the LORD, abuse the sacrifices at Shiloh and treat the LORD’s offering with contempt.

verses.text: Elkanah went to Ramah to his house. The child served the LORD before Eli the priest.
verses.arminianNotes: Elkanah returns to Ramah, and the child serves the LORD before Eli. Arminian readers see Samuel beginning his service as the fulfillment of Hannah’s vow.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s purpose for Samuel unfolding. The quiet note about the child’s service sets him in contrast with Eli’s sons, described in the next verse.

verses.text: Now the sons of Eli were wicked men. They didn’t know the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: “Now the sons of Eli were wicked men. They didn’t know the LORD.” Arminian readers see priests who held office without genuine relationship with God and who are responsible for that failure.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the tragedy of religious office without true knowledge of God. The verse is mostly shared ground: privilege and position do not replace a heart that knows the LORD.

verses.text: The custom of the priests with the people was that when anyone offered a sacrifice, the priest’s servant came while the meat was boiling, with a fork of three teeth in his hand;
verses.arminianNotes: The priests’ servant comes with a three-pronged fork while the meat is boiling. Arminian readers see a custom that turns sacred worship into an opportunity for personal gain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the corruption of priestly practice. The detailed description shows how the abuse became an established routine at the sanctuary.

verses.text: and he stabbed it into the pan, or kettle, or cauldron, or pot. The priest took all that the fork brought up for himself. They did this to all the Israelites who came there to Shiloh.
verses.arminianNotes: The priest takes whatever the fork brings up from the pot, and they do this to all who come to Shiloh. Arminian readers see worshipers wronged by those who should have served them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the priests taking more than God allotted them. The Law assigned specific portions to priests, as in Leviticus 7:31–34, and this grabbing disregards those limits.

verses.text: Yes, before they burned the fat, the priest’s servant came, and said to the man who sacrificed, “Give meat to roast for the priest; for he will not accept boiled meat from you, but raw.”
verses.arminianNotes: Before the fat is burned, the servant demands, “Give meat to roast for the priest.” Arminian readers see contempt for God shown in seizing meat before God’s portion is offered.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a serious offense, since the fat belonged to the LORD according to Leviticus 3:16. The priests put their own appetite ahead of God’s honor.

verses.text: If the man said to him, “Let the fat be burned first, and then take as much as your soul desires;” then he would say, “No, but you shall give it to me now; and if not, I will take it by force.”
verses.arminianNotes: When a worshiper asks, “Let the fat be burned first,” the servant replies, “No, but you shall give it to me now; and if not, I will take it by force.” Arminian readers see coercion of faithful people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see worshipers trying to honor God while the priests resort to threats. The contrast between lay piety and priestly abuse sharpens the indictment.

verses.text: The sin of the young men was very great before the LORD; for the men despised the LORD’s offering.
verses.arminianNotes: “The sin of the young men was very great before the LORD; for the men despised the LORD’s offering.” Arminian readers see their guilt measured by contempt for what God had commanded.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s verdict on their behavior. This verdict is shared ground: misusing worship is not merely a social wrong but a sin directly against the LORD.
